_comment: SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for the error taxonomy. Both halves of the system read this.
Python reads it directly (progress/taxonomy.py). The web app CANNOT — Vercel deploys
from web/ and never uploads files above it — so it reads a copy at
web/lib/progress/taxonomy.json, which is generated by `python scripts/sync_taxonomy.py`.
EDIT THIS FILE, THEN RUN THAT SCRIPT. Editing the copy directly will be overwritten.
If they drift, the dashboard falls back to showing the raw category key instead of a
label — degraded, not broken, and the sync script's --check mode will tell you.
`hint` is for the grading LLM (it goes into the prompt). `label` and `advice` are for
the learner. Adding a category here makes it available to the grader, the weak-areas
chart, and the practice suggestions with no other code change.

categories.label: Verb tenses
categories.hint: wrong or inconsistent tense: 'I go there yesterday', 'I am knowing him'
categories.advice: Tell a story about your weekend in the past tense, then tell it again as if it were happening right now. Switching deliberately makes the tenses stick.

categories.label: Subject–verb agreement
categories.hint: subject and verb do not agree in number: 'she go', 'they was', 'he don't'
categories.advice: Practice describing what other people do — 'he works', 'she takes', 'they run'. Third-person singular is where the -s goes missing most.

categories.label: Articles (a / an / the)
categories.hint: missing, extra, or wrong article: 'I saw movie', 'the life is hard'
categories.advice: Describe the room you're in out loud, naming every object with 'a' or 'the'. Ask yourself each time: does the listener already know which one I mean?

categories.label: Prepositions
categories.hint: wrong preposition: 'depends of', 'married with', 'on the morning'
categories.advice: Prepositions rarely follow rules — they come in fixed pairs. Collect the ones you get wrong as whole phrases ('depend ON', 'arrive AT') and reuse them in conversation rather than memorising them.

categories.label: Plurals and countability
categories.hint: plural/singular or countability error: 'many informations', 'two childs'
categories.advice: Practice with the awkward uncountables — advice, information, furniture, news, research. Say 'a piece of advice' until 'an advice' starts to sound wrong.

categories.label: Word order
categories.hint: words in the wrong order: 'I know not', 'always he is late'
categories.advice: English holds subject-verb-object hard. Practice placing adverbs — 'he is always late', not 'always he is late' — since that's where word order usually slips.

categories.label: Forming questions
categories.hint: malformed question: 'What you are doing?', 'Do you went?'
categories.advice: Ask Ahmad five questions in a row on purpose. Questions invert the subject and auxiliary, and that inversion is easy to skip when you're speaking fast.

categories.label: Pronouns
categories.hint: wrong or missing pronoun: 'me and him went', 'is raining'
categories.advice: Watch for the dropped subject — English needs one even when it means nothing ('it is raining'). Many languages don't, so this transfers straight across.

categories.label: Modal verbs
categories.hint: misused modal: 'I must to go', 'I can to swim', 'you should going'
categories.advice: A modal is always followed by a bare verb: 'must go', never 'must to go'. Practice talking about obligations and possibilities in your own life.

categories.label: Conditionals
categories.hint: broken if-clause: 'If I will see him, I tell her'
categories.advice: Talk through hypotheticals — what you'd do if you won money, moved abroad, could start over. Conditionals only get comfortable when the topic is imaginary.

categories.label: Word choice
categories.hint: grammatically fine but the wrong or unnatural word: 'I did a mistake', 'open the light'
categories.advice: These are collocations — words that habitually travel together. 'Make a mistake', 'turn on the light'. Notice the pairing, not the individual word.

categories.label: Comparatives and superlatives
categories.advice: Compare things out loud — cities you've lived in, food you've eaten. Short words take -er/-est, long words take more/most, and never both at once.
